en: Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities.
Om! Homage to the Blessed Lady, the Noble Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Homage to the Noble Mañjuśrī.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, in order to gladden those four assemblies, once again elucidating this Perfection of Wisdom, at that time spoke these verses:
"Having established supreme love, reverence, and serene faith, having abandoned all obscurations, and having transcended the stains of the afflictions—
listen, O you who have set out for the sake of the world!"
Wherein the heroes practice the perfection of wisdom of those [three vehicles]. // Rgs_1.1 //
As many rivers as flow here in Jambudvīpa, which cause fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs,
and forest trees to grow,
all depend upon the earth, the lord of elephants, and the sovereign of serpents.
Such was the majestic power and splendor of that Lord of Beings.
Whatever dharmas the Jina’s disciples teach, speak, or proclaim with logical consistency;
the performance of the activity that brings about ultimate happiness and the attainment of its fruit—all this is the Tathāgata’s human effort (puruṣakāra).

For what reason? Because those disciples of the Bull among Men who have been consecrated therein, having directly realized the way of Dharma that the Victor has taught, teach it according to how they were trained—both through the power of the Buddhas and further through the power of their own strength.
In which there is no apprehension of the supreme perfection of wisdom, nor apprehension of a bodhisattva, nor of the awakening of the mind—
having heard this, he who is neither deluded nor terrified, that bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the Sugatas.
For him there is not even an atom’s worth of a station for form, feeling, perception, volition, or consciousness;
established in no dharma and wandering without a home, he who is ungrasping attains the enlightenment of the Sugatas.
Then Śreṇika, the wandering mendicant, attained knowledge and the realization that the aggregates are not to be conceptualized;
the Bodhisattva who thoroughly understands these phenomena in this way does not touch nirvāṇa, and thus he dwells in wisdom.
Furthermore, he investigates: "In what [categories] does wisdom reside? Why? From where do all these phenomena arise as empty?
While investigating thus, he does not sink down nor does he feel terror; that bodhisattva becomes near to awakening.
If a bodhisattva courses in the aggregates of form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness without understanding them,
yet conceives of these aggregates as empty, he courses in the signless and unarisen state, unattached.
He does not course in form, feeling, perception, volition, or consciousness; he courses without a fixed abode.
The bearer of wisdom does not adhere to the notion that "he courses"; being without grasping, he touches the peace of the supreme samādhi.
Thus dwelling here in the peace of the self, that bodhisattva has been prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past;
yet he does not conceive the thought, "I have emerged from samādhi," because he has thoroughly understood the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Practicing in this way, one practices the wisdom of the Sugatas, yet one does not apprehend even that dharma in which one practices.
Having understood both practice and non-practice, this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
That which does not exist is this very non-existence; the fool, imagining it, creates ignorance where there is no knowledge.
Both knowledge and ignorance are non-existent phenomena; the Bodhisattva who understands that they emerge [in this way] is truly wise. Rgs 1.13.
He who understands that the five aggregates here are like an illusion, and does not conceive of the illusion as one thing and the aggregates as another;
being free from the perception of multiplicity and walking in tranquility—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
For one who possesses spiritual friends and practices insight, no fear will arise upon hearing the measure of the Victors;
but he who is accompanied by evil friends and is led by others is like an unbaked clay vessel shattered when touched by water.

For what reason is this one called a "bodhisattva"? Because he desires to sever all attachments everywhere; he will touch the unattached awakening of the Victors, and for that very reason, he receives the name "bodhisattva. (Rgs 1.16)
For what great reason is he called a "Mahāsattva" (Great Being) here for the sake of this mass of beings?
Because he cuts through the great range of views within the realm of beings, for that reason, O Mahāsattva, he is so called.

The great leader, of vast intelligence and great majesty, mounted upon the samādhi of the supreme Victors of the Mahāyāna—having girded himself with great armor, he shall subdue the deceitful Namuci; for that reason, he is called a "Great Being" (mahāsattva). Rgs 1.18.

Just as a magician, having conjured a great multitude of beings at a crossroads, cuts off many millions of heads, yet knows those beings to be an illusion—knowing all sentient beings to be such a magical creation of the world—he feels no fear. Rgs 1.19.
Form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated, being unattached;
thus does awakening proceed, with a mind that is not dejected—this is the armor of the most excellent of supreme persons.
For what reason is this called the vehicle of awakening? Having ascended it, one brings all sentient beings to extinction.
This vehicle is equal to space, a great celestial palace; it is the supreme vehicle that leads to the attainment of happiness, bliss, and security.

And no one is found who goes by ascending toward the direction of the attainment of nirvāṇa; such a course is unapprehendable. Just as when a fire is extinguished, it has no movement of going, for that reason it is called "extinguished. (Rgs 1.22)
A bodhisattva is not apprehended from the past limit, nor even from the future limit; he is pure throughout the three times.
That which is pure is unconditioned and free from conceptual proliferation—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
And at whatever time a wise bodhisattva, having reflected thus upon non-arising,
practices in this way and generates great compassion while yet lacking the notion of a "sentient being"— this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
If, based on the perception of a "being" and the perception of "suffering," one thinks, "I shall remove the suffering of the world and I shall bring about its welfare"—
that bodhisattva is one who conceptualizes a self and a being; this is not the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
As he understands himself, so he understands all sentient beings; as he understands all sentient beings, so he understands all phenomena.
Without conceptualizing either non-arising or arising, this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

Having transcended all the names of dharmas proclaimed in the world, one realizes the supreme gnosis known as the Deathless; that which is not surpassed by anything else, having a single meaning with wisdom—this is what is called "Perfection."

Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva has no doubt; one who knows how to dwell thus possesses both skillful means and wisdom. Fully understanding that all phenomena are by nature non-existent—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the first chapter, titled "The Practice of the Knowledge of All Aspects."
He who does not abide in form, nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in volition;
he who does not abide in consciousness, but abides in the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
The permanent and impermanent, pleasure and pain, the auspicious and inauspicious—these are non-self within the self; likewise, they are suchness within emptiness.
Established in the attainment of the fruit, he stands upon the stage of the Arhat, established upon the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, and likewise upon the stage of the Buddha.

Just as the Leader does not abide in the unconditioned realm, so too he does not abide in the conditioned; wandering without a fixed abode, the Bodhisattva thus stands without standing. This non-abiding is the standing spoken of by the Jina.

Whoever desires, "May I become a disciple of the Sugata, or likewise a Pratyekabuddha, or a King of Dharma," cannot attain this patient acceptance without seeing what has passed, just as one who wishes to go from this shore to the further shore [cannot do so without a boat]. Rgs 2.4.
Whoever speaks the Dharma, whoever will speak it, and those who have attained the fruit while it is being spoken— the Pratyekabuddhas and likewise the Lords of the World—
who have realized nirvāṇa through their wisdom and learning, all of them are seen by the Tathāgata as his own children.

O Son of the Conqueror, these four types of persons do not tremble in this [teaching]: the one skilled in the truths, the irreversible, the Arhat whose stains and afflictions have been shaken off and whose doubts have been abandoned, and the fourth, who has been ripened by a spiritual friend.
Practicing in this way, the wise and learned Bodhisattva does not train for the level of a Śrāvaka nor for the level of a Pratyekabuddha;
he trains for omniscience and in the Buddha-dharmas. That which is neither training nor non-training—this is true training.
They do not train for the sake of grasping at the increase or decrease of form, nor do they train for the sake of grasping at various phenomena;
yet, while training, they grasp after omniscience and thus go forth—this is the training of those who delight in these virtues.
Wisdom does not exist in form; wisdom does not exist in that which possesses form, nor in consciousness, perception, feeling, or volition.
Wisdom does not come from them, nor does it exist within them; it is equal to the element of space and has no differentiation.

The nature of objective referents is boundless; the nature of sentient beings is also boundless. The nature of the realm of space is boundless, and the wisdom of the Knower of the World is likewise boundless.
"Perception"—this is the name proclaimed by the Leader. Having analyzed perception and proceeding toward its abandonment, they reach the further shore.
Those who here attain the departure from perception have reached the further shore; they abide in the perfection. (Rgs 2.11)

Even if one were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, proclaiming the word "sentient being," thinking, "This is the Leader," or "How will a sentient being become primordially pure?"— this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

Thus the Jina speaks, he whose speech is never contrary: "When I abided in this supreme perfection, I was then prophesied by another Supreme Person: 'In a future time, you shall become a Buddha. (Rgs 2.13)
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the second chapter, titled "Śakra."
Whoever shall take up this [perfection] and master it will always practice the perfection of wisdom wherein the Protectors course;
poison, fire, weapons, and water cannot overcome them, nor can Māra find an opening, nor the faction of Māra.
Suppose someone were to build stūpas made of the seven precious gems for the Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa and worship them;
may thousands of millions of fields be completely filled with such stūpas of the Sugata, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Furthermore, suppose as many beings as there are in those millions of fields were all to perform worship for infinite eons—with divine flowers, excellent perfumes, and ointments—for eons as numerous as the conceptualizations of the three times; even more than that—*Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* 3.3.
And whoever, having written this Mother of the Sugatas in a book— from which the Guides endowed with the ten powers arise—
should preserve it and honor it with flowers and ointments, their merit would not be a mere fraction compared to that of one who has built a stūpa and performed worship.
This great vidyā, the perfection of wisdom, pacifies the suffering, phenomena, and sorrow of beings within the vast realm of sentient beings;
those who were the Lords of the World in the past, and those in the ten directions, were supreme Kings of Physicians who trained in this vidyā.
Those who practice here with conduct characterized by benefit and compassion, O wise one trained in knowledge, shall touch enlightenment.
Whatever conditioned happiness there is, and whatever unconditioned happiness there may be—all such happiness should be known as having originated from this.
Seeds scattered upon the earth come into being; having obtained the necessary conditions, they grow in many forms.
So too do all the qualities of enlightenment and the five perfections grow through the perfection of wisdom.
Just as a universal monarch proceeds with his entire army and all seven precious jewels,
so too do all qualities and dharmas come together through this perfection of wisdom of the Victors.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the third chapter, titled "The Veneration of the Stūpa of the Perfection of Holding Immeasurable Qualities."

Śakra asked the Jina a question: "If there were Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all the relics of the Jinas were filled and bound together as a single crest-ornament, one should grasp this very supreme perfection of wisdom."
What is the reason? It is not that there is a lack of respect for my physical body; rather, it is because they honor that which is permeated by wisdom.
Just as a person who relies upon a king receives all honors, so too does the Buddha-nature rely upon the perfection of wisdom.

A precious jewel endowed with all virtues, having attained an incalculable value, is worthy of veneration even when it remains within its casket; yet people long for it even when it has been taken out, for those qualities belong to that very great jewel itself. Rgs 4.3.
In the same way, the supreme qualities of the perfection of wisdom are such that even after the Victor has passed into nirvāṇa, his relics receive worship.
Therefore, one who desires to grasp those qualities of the Victor should take up this perfection of wisdom; this is liberation.
Let giving be the precursor; let them give, and likewise wisdom, ethical discipline, patience, as well as vigor and meditative concentration.
It is the sustainer that prevents the loss of wholesome qualities, and it alone reveals all phenomena.
Just as in Jambudvīpa there are many thousands of millions of trees— of various kinds, diverse, and of many forms—
their shadows do not become distinct in their variety, except when one speaks of them by way of counting the shadows themselves.
In the same way, these five perfections of the Victors become known as the perfection of wisdom;
when all six are dedicated toward omniscience, they reach the single method called awakening.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, the fourth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities," is concluded.
If a bodhisattva, even regarding form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness, transforms the mind toward impermanence,
yet practices according to a mere semblance without true understanding, the wise one never brings about the destruction of the Dharma.
In that which there is no form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor consciousness, nor even the apprehension of volition;
where one knows all phenomena as unarisen and empty—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
Even if someone were to discipline as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges rivers throughout all those realms,
the merit of one who writes down this perfection of wisdom and gives the book to other beings is far more distinguished.
For what reason? Because those best of speakers, having trained here, cause all dharmas to be understood within emptiness;
hearing which, the śrāvakas quickly touch liberation and attain both the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas and the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Just as there is no arising of a tree from a non-existent sprout in this world, how could there be the production of branches, leaves, fruit, and flowers?
Likewise, without the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), there is no arising of a Victor in the world; how could there be the appearance of Śakra, Brahmā, or the fruit of the Śrāvaka?
Just as when the solar disc emits a web of light, beings exert themselves in their various activities;
so too, the thought of awakening, once known by the Knower of the World, brings about the convergence of all qualities and dharmas through wisdom.
Just as there would be no heat from a non-existent serpent-king, how could there be a river’s flow here in Jambudvīpa?
Without a river, fruits and flowers would not come to be; nor would the oceans possess jewels of manifold forms. (Rgs 5.7)
Likewise, if the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) does not exist here, how could the flow of the Tathāgata’s wisdom arise in this entire world?
And if wisdom does not exist, there is no increase in qualities; there would be neither awakening equal to the ocean nor the Buddha-qualities.

Whatever luminous beings there may be anywhere in the world who emit light for the sake of illumination—all those splendors together would not equal even a fraction of a single ray emitted from the excellent orb of the sun; such is the radiance of all the hosts of stars.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the fifth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of Merit."
Whatever merit the hosts of śrāvakas produce— whether through generosity, ethical discipline, or that which is associated with mental cultivation—
a single moment of a bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy exceeds the entire mass of merit belonging to all those hosts of śrāvakas.
Those millions of billions of Buddhas who have passed away in the past, those in infinite thousands of millions of fields,
and those Lords of the World who currently abide or have entered final nirvana— they all teach the jewel of the Dharma for the sake of the exhaustion of suffering.

From the first generation of the mind set on supreme enlightenment until the time when the Dharma of the Guides has utterly perished—whatever merit belongs to those Victors therein, together with the perfections and all the Buddha-qualities, all that is joined as one. (Rgs 6.3)

Whatever wholesome roots of the sons of the Buddha and of the Śrāvakas— whether they be those of the learners (*śaikṣa*) or the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—
the Bodhisattva, having gathered them all together, rejoices in them and dedicates it all for the sake of awakening as the cause for the welfare of the world.
If there is the perception of a mind, or likewise the perception of a being in the dedication of a bodhisattva,

then because the mind remains fixed on the view of those perceptions and is joined with the three attachments, that which is being dedicated does not become a true dedication as long as it is being apprehended.
If one knows that as soon as it arises, it ceases, and that all phenomena are exhausted, and if they dedicate that which is exhausted toward that [enlightenment],
yet never conceive of a phenomenon as dedicating a phenomenon— when one understands in this way, it is truly dedicated.
If one creates a sign and does not honor it, then [that merit] becomes dedicated to enlightenment through the signless.
Just as food mixed with poison, though prepared with excellent ingredients, is so described by the Victor, so too is the apprehension of white dharmas.
Therefore, one should indeed train in the transformation of names, just as those Victors understand that very merit—
its nature, its source, and its characteristic— and in whatever way they do so, in that same way I rejoice and transform it.
Thus dedicating merit toward awakening, he does not indeed disparage the Buddha who speaks as a Victor;
surpassing all those bodhisattvas in the world who perceive objects through apprehension, the hero excels them all by means of this dedication.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the sixth chapter, titled "Rejoicing."
Millions of billions of those born blind, lacking a guide, are unskilled in the path; how could they enter the city?
Without wisdom, these five perfections are sightless and without a guide; they are not capable of touching enlightenment.
When one has grasped wisdom within, one obtains this name "One Who Has Attained the Eye.
It is like a person who, though skilled in the completion of a painting, possesses no eyes; as long as he has not provided eyes for it, he does not receive the merit [of his work]. Rgs 7.2.
When, through the discernment of wisdom, one does not perceive even an atom of conditioned or unconditioned phenomena, whether dark or light;
when one enters into the reckoning of the perfection of wisdom in the world, there is nothing therein that is established, just as in space.

If he thinks, "I practice the wisdom of the Victors; I shall liberate millions of beings afflicted by many diseases," that bodhisattva is merely conceptualizing the notion of a "being," and this is not the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

The bodhisattva who has practiced the supreme perfection and who, being wise, feels no doubt when hearing it from others— toward him there will arise the perception of a Teacher, and he will swiftly awaken to peaceful enlightenment.

Having honored millions of Buddhas while serving them, yet lacking faith in the perfection of wisdom of the Victors, that person of small intelligence will reject it upon hearing it; having rejected it, he will go to the Avīci hell, becoming one who has no protector.
Therefore, indeed, have faith in the mothers of the Victors if you wish to touch the supreme wisdom of a Buddha;
otherwise, one would be like a merchant who, having gone to the island of jewels, returns again after cutting off his own roots.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the seventh chapter, titled "Hell."
The purity of form should be understood from the purity of its fruit; they say that from the purity of the fruit, which is the nature of form, comes the purity of omniscience.
From the purity of the fruit of omniscience, the purity of form is inseparable and indivisible from the equality of the realm of space.
Having transcended the triple world, the Bodhisattvas do not abandon their afflictions, yet they manifest rebirth;
free from old age, sickness, and death, they demonstrate passing away—this is where the wise ones practice the perfection of wisdom.
Just as this world of form is stuck in the mud, it revolves in the wheel of saṃsāra like a wind-driven wheel;
having understood that the world is deluded like a snare for deer, the wise roam about like birds in the sky.

He who does not course in form, but courses in complete purity regarding perception, consciousness, feeling, and volition—coursing thus, he avoids all attachments; freed from attachment, he courses in the wisdom of the Sugatas.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the eighth chapter, titled "Purity."
Practicing in this way, the wise and learned Bodhisattva, having severed all attachments, proceeds through the world unattached;
like the sun released from the grasp of Rāhu, he shines brilliantly, and like a well-kindled fire, he consumes the forest of grass and wood.

Through wisdom, the bodhisattva perceives all phenomena as naturally pure and utterly cleansed; yet he finds neither a perceiver nor any phenomena—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom. (Rgs 9.2)
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the ninth chapter, titled "Praise."
Śakra, the king of the gods, questioned the Jina: "How does a bodhisattva practice when engaged in wisdom? [The Buddha replied:
"He who is not attached even to the slightest degree to the aggregates and the elements—he who is thus unattached, he is a bodhisattva."
That being who has set out on the long journey should be known as one who has performed his service under many millions of billions of Buddhas;
for having heard these teachings which are like emanations and illusions, he does not waver, and thus, while training, he applies himself to practice.

When a person on a path through the wilderness sees many people, cowherds, boundaries, and the abundance of forests, he becomes one who has attained reassurance; he has no fear, for these are the signs that villages and cities are near. (Rgs 10.3)
In the same way, O dear one, listen to how one who seeks awakening and attains the supreme perfection of wisdom of the Victors finds consolation;
for such a person there is no fear, nor is there the stage of an Arhat, nor even the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.

For when a person goes to see the waters of the ocean, he may see trees, forests, and the king of mountains; or he may not see them, yet he becomes free from doubt that the great ocean is not far away. (Rgs 10.5)
In the same way, one who has set out for the supreme enlightenment should be known as such while hearing this perfection of wisdom of the Victors;
even if they have not been prophesied to it by the Leader in his presence, nevertheless, they will soon touch the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Just as when spring arrives, grass, leaves, and branches do not long before they are joined with foliage, fruit, and flowers;
so too, for one who has this perfection of wisdom in the palm of their hand, they will before long attain supreme enlightenment among the Leaders.
Just as a pregnant woman who experiences [certain] movements knows that it is time for her to give birth,
so too the Bodhisattva, hearing the wisdom of the Victors, perceives joy and zeal and will swiftly touch enlightenment.
The yogi practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom perceives neither the increase of form nor its diminution;
seeing phenomena as non-phenomena, this realm of phenomena, he does not touch nirvana, but dwells in wisdom.

He who, while practicing here, does not conceptualize the qualities of a Buddha, nor conceptualizes the powers, the bases of psychic power, or peaceful awakening; free from conceptualization and non-conceptualization, moving by means of empowerment—this is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Qualities of the Dhāraṇī."
Subhūti asks the Buddha, the moon among speakers: "How long will the lifespan be for those who delight in virtuous qualities?
The Teacher says: "It will be very long; I shall describe it to you only in brief."
While one is writing this perfection of wisdom of the Victors, various and manifold flashes of inspired eloquence will arise;
yet, like a flash of lightning, they will quickly vanish, failing to accomplish the welfare of the world—this is the work of Māra. (Rgs 11.2)

And some will have doubts while I am speaking; for the Leader has not proclaimed my name here, nor has he proclaimed my birthplace or my clan. One who does not hear this will reject it; that is the work of Māra.

Thus, having abandoned the root, those deluded ones, not knowing [it], will search for the branches and leaves; just as one who, having found an elephant, would go searching for its footprints, so too, having heard the Perfection of Wisdom, they will seek it in other sūtras. Rgs 11.4.
Just as someone, having obtained food of a hundred flavors on the way, might receive sixty kinds of that supreme food;
so too the Bodhisattva, having obtained these perfections, [abides] on the stage of an Arhat.
They will seek after awakening.
They will desire honor and seek gain; with minds full of attachment, they will be intent on intimacy with noble families.
Having abandoned the Dharma, they will perform unrighteous deeds; having left the true path, they have entered upon a wrong path—this is the work of Māra.
And those who at that time shall conceive a desire and faith to hear this supreme Dharma,
the Dharma-preachers, perceiving them to be occupied with their affairs and devoid of affection, will depart with very heavy hearts.
In that time, there will be these works of Māra and many other various and numerous obstacles;
by these, many monks will be so distracted that they do not uphold this perfection of wisdom. (Rgs 11.8)
Those jewels that exist which have attained such value that they are beyond price are difficult to find and are constantly beset by many adversaries;
even so, this supreme perfection of wisdom—the jewel of the Dharma of the Victors—is difficult to obtain and fraught with many obstacles.

Those beings who have newly set out in the vehicle and possess limited intelligence, yet attain this jewel of the Dharma so difficult to find—Māra will become eager to create obstacles for them; however, the Buddhas of the ten directions are engaged in their protection.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra."
O son, there are many illnesses in the body; all those [illnesses] would cause one to be dejected and apply oneself to them.
In the same way, even though there are Buddhas in the world-systems of the ten directions, they attend only to this Perfection of Wisdom.
Those who were the Lords of the World in the past, those who are in the ten directions now, and those who will arise in the future—they are all born from this [Perfection of Wisdom].
She is the mother who reveals the world to the Victors, and she is the one who demonstrates the mental conduct of other beings.
The suchness of the world is the suchness of Arhats;
the suchness of Pratyekabuddhas is the suchness of the Jinas.
This single suchness, devoid of intrinsic being, is none other than the perfection of wisdom, O Buddha, Tathāgata.
Let alone those who know the world who have entered final nirvāṇa—this fixed order of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains as empty phenomena.
Bodhisattvas awaken to that suchness; therefore, the name "Buddha" was bestowed upon them by the Tathāgatas.
This is the domain of the Guides, the possessors of the ten powers, who dwell in the delightful forest of the perfection of wisdom;
they rescue suffering beings from the three lower realms, yet never do they harbor even the notion of a "being" toward them.
Just as a lion, having taken refuge in a mountain cave, roars without fear, terrifying the small, inferior animals;
so too does the lion among men, relying on the perfection of wisdom, roar without fear, terrifying the many heretics.
Just as the sun’s rays, resting in space, heat this earth and reveal forms,
so too the King of Dharma, relying on the perfection of wisdom, heats the river of craving and reveals the Dharma.
The non-seeing of form and the non-seeing of feeling, the non-seeing of perception and the non-seeing of volition,
and the non-seeing of consciousness and mind— where these do not exist, that is the vision of phenomena taught by the Tathāgata.
"Space is seen," so beings proclaim; but how can one see the sky? Reflect upon this meaning!
In the same way, the vision of the Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata; for it cannot be described by means of any visible object.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the World."

He who sees thus sees all phenomena as the king [sees] all the activities of his ministers with equanimity; by means of wisdom, he performs all those activities of the Buddhas and the nature of reality belonging to the Śrāvakas that are contained within the perfection of wisdom. Rgs 13.1.
The king does not go to the villages nor to the kingdoms and provinces, yet he takes all revenue from his domain;
likewise, the Bodhisattva does not move at all from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), yet he takes up all those qualities that constitute the Buddha-dharma.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Inconceivable."
The Bodhisattva who possesses firm faith in the Sugata and is endowed with the intention for the supreme perfection of wisdom,
having transcended the two levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, will swiftly attain the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Victors.

Just as a hired laborer on a leaking ship at sea who does not take up grass and wood for support perishes in the midst of the water without reaching the shore, whereas he who does take them up reaches the dry land on the other side; Rgs 14.2.
In the very same way, those who have entered into faith and attained serene confidence, yet abandon the perfection of wisdom alone,
will perpetually wander in the ocean of saṃsāra, amidst the breaking waves of birth, old age, death, and sorrow.
Those who are embraced by excellent wisdom, who are skilled in the intrinsic nature of phenomena, and who perceive the ultimate truth—
they possess the vessel of the ship that is the accumulation of the wealth of merit and knowledge, and they swiftly touch the most wonderful awakening of the Sugata.
Just as if someone were to carry uncooked water in a jar, one should know that it will soon break due to its fragility;
but carrying cooked water in a jar along the road, one encounters no fear of breaking and reaches home in safety. Rgs 14.5.
Even if a bodhisattva should abound in faith, if they are devoid of wisdom, they will quickly come to ruin;
yet by embracing that very same faith and transcending through wisdom, they will attain the two types of awakening and the supreme enlightenment.

Just as a ship that has not been properly prepared perishes at sea along with its wealth and its merchants, yet that very same ship, when well-prepared and well-fastened, does not break apart and reaches the shore with all its cargo intact; so it is with the Dharma-ship. Rgs_14.7 //
In the same way, a bodhisattva who is cultivated by faith but lacks wisdom quickly suffers a loss regarding enlightenment;
yet one who is properly engaged in the supreme perfection of wisdom remains unhurt and unharmed, and touches the enlightenment of the Victors.

For a man who is aged, suffering, and two hundred years old, even if he has risen by himself, he is not able to go; yet, when supported on both his left and right sides by two men, he has no fear of falling and travels with ease. Rgs 14.9.
In the same way, a bodhisattva here who lacks wisdom may set out, yet he breaks down along the way;
but one who is embraced by the power of skillful means and wisdom does not break down, and touches the awakening of the bulls among men.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Similes."

The wise Bodhisattva who stands at the stage of initial action and has set out with superior resolve for the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha should always serve spiritual friends, being endowed with excellent discipleship and reverence for the teacher.
For what reason? Because the arrival of qualities for the wise comes from them; they instruct [them] in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus the Victor, the bearer of the foremost of all qualities, says: "The Buddha-qualities depend upon reliance on a spiritual friend."
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, as well as vigor, meditative concentrations, and wisdom should be dedicated toward awakening;
yet, having analyzed the aggregates of awakening, one should not grasp at them, nor should one teach it in this way to beginners.

Practicing in this way, these oceans of virtue, moons among speakers, become the protection, the refuge, and the shelter for the world; they are the goal, the intelligence, the island, and the guide, desiring the welfare of others—unshakable lamps and torches who proclaim the sublime Dharma.
The one of great renown dons the armor of what is difficult to do; yet they do not don it by means of the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields.
Free from the notion of the three vehicles, ungrasping, irreversible, immovable, and of an unshakable nature—Rgs 15.5.

Those very ones who have fully realized the Dharma, free from conceptual proliferation, devoid of doubt, hesitation, and uncertainty, and endowed with the meaning of reality—having heard the perfection of wisdom, they do not despair; they should be known as those who are not led by others and are irreversible.
This profound Dharma of the Leaders is difficult to see; it has not been realized by anyone, nor do they attain it.
Having realized this awakening, the one who is compassionate for the welfare of others remains free from anxiety; who among the multitude of beings will understand this?

Beings who delight in the *ālaya*, who crave sense objects, and who remain in grasping—being ignorant and utterly blinded—a conflict has arisen with the world regarding the Dharma that is to be attained as non-*ālaya* and free from grasping. Rgs 15.8.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Gods."

The element of space in the eastern direction, and likewise in the south, west, and north—boundless and shoreless—is the same from above and below throughout the ten directions; it possesses no diversity, nor does it attain any distinction.
The suchness that has passed away, the suchness that has not been reached, and the suchness of the present—this is the suchness of the Arhats.
That which is the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the Arhats; the suchness of all phenomena does not possess any distinction.
The bodhisattva who wishes to attain the enlightenment of the Sugatas, which is free from the phenomena of diversity, should apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom;
for without being joined to this wisdom, there is no realization of the Leaders of Men.
Suppose there were a bird with a body a hundred yojanas in size, yet its wings were both worn out and powerless;
even if it wished to descend from the abodes of the Thirty-three Gods to Jambudvīpa, it would perish in mid-air. (Rgs 16.4)
Even if one were to fully accomplish these five perfections of the Victors for many hundreds of billions of eons,
and while constantly cultivating infinite and vast aspirations, if one lacks skillful means and is devoid of wisdom in this world, one will end up as a śrāvaka.
One who desires to set forth toward the wisdom of a Buddha should regard all beings with an even mind, as if they were one's own father or mother;
with a benevolent heart and a mind of loving-kindness, one should exert oneself; being entirely upright and gentle in speech, one should exert oneself.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the sixteenth chapter, titled "Suchness."
The Elder Subhūti questioned the Lord of the World: "Speak of the mark of passionlessness for those who are oceans of virtue;
explain even a mere fraction of the qualities of a Jina, by which those of great majesty become irreversible."
Free from perceptions of diversity, they speak with propriety; they do not rely on other ascetics or brahmins.
These wise ones are forever free from the three lower realms and are endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action.
They teach the Dharma to the world without worldly motive, being always fixed in the absolute Dharma and speaking with gentle words;
whether standing, walking, lying down, or sitting, they remain fully aware, and as they walk, they look only a yoke’s length ahead with undistracted thought.
Wearing pure and clean garments, purified by the three kinds of discernment, they never desire gain; being bulls of the Dharma, they always long for the Dharma.
Having transcended the spheres of Māra, they cannot be led astray by others; they meditate upon the four dhyānas, yet they do not rely upon those dhyānas.
They do not desire fame, nor is their mind overcome by anger; having become householders, they are never attached to any material thing.
They do not seek livelihoods through the objects of sensory enjoyment, nor do they employ mantras for sorcery or mantras for the practice of women.

Those who are intent upon the supreme perfection of wisdom do not desire women through men, being free from quarrels and disputes; possessing firm minds of loving-kindness, they always incline their hearts toward the teaching out of a desire for omniscience.
They avoid borderlands and regions inhabited by barbarians; they have no longing for their own lands and are always like Mount Meru.
Devoted to yoga, they sacrifice even their lives for the sake of the Dharma. These should be known as the marks of those who are irreversible.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Signs and Forms of Irreversibility."
Form, feeling, volition, consciousness, and perception are by nature signless and peaceful;
like one seeking a footing in the ocean with a staff, when one examines the aggregates with wisdom, no footing is found.

The Bodhisattva who awakens to these very phenomena—which are profound, the ultimate truth of the vehicle, and untainted—in which there are no aggregates, nor sense-bases, nor elements, what could there be for him of his own accumulated merit? (Rgs 18.2)
Just as a man whose nature is dominated by passion might make an appointment with a woman and then fail to meet her,
so too does a bodhisattva awaken to as many eons as there are mental activities in a single day.
If a bodhisattva were to give pure gifts for many thousands of millions of eons, and likewise maintain ethical discipline, compared to one who,
engaged in the supreme perfection of wisdom, should speak the Dharma— the merit of the former would not equal even a fraction of the latter’s.
The Bodhisattva who, manifesting supreme wisdom, rises from that state and teaches the stainless Dharma,
and dedicates even that for the sake of awakening as the cause for the welfare of the world— for him there is no merit in the three worlds equal to it.
And that very merit is further declared to be empty, void, hollow, vain, and without essence.
Practicing in this way, one practices the wisdom of the Sugatas; while practicing thus, one grasps immeasurable merit.
One knows that all these phenomena are mere verbal expressions, taught, applied, and revealed by the Buddha;
even if one were to speak of them for many millions of billions of eons, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) would neither diminish nor increase.
These five perfections of the Victors are also proclaimed as dharmas that are merely names;
the Bodhisattva dedicates them and does not conceive of them, and thus he does not fall away, but touches the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the eighteenth chapter, titled "Emptiness.

When a wick is set ablaze with oil, the wick is not consumed by the first incidence [of the flame], nor is it consumed without that [incidence]. Indeed, the wick is not consumed by the final incidence of the flame; yet, even without the final [flame], the lamp-wick is not burned. (Rgs 19.1)
The first thought does not touch supreme enlightenment, for it is non-existent; once it has ceased to exist, it can no longer touch it.
Nor does the final thought reach the state of peace, for it is non-existent; once it has ceased to exist, it can no longer reach it.
From a seed, the stalk, fruit, and flowers arise; yet that seed has ceased and does not exist, for there is no tree belonging to it.
Just so, the mind is the primary cause of enlightenment; yet that mind has ceased and does not exist, for there is no enlightenment belonging to it.
Depending upon a seed, there arise various fruits such as barley or rice; yet that fruit neither exists nor does it not exist.
From such arising comes this awakening of the Victors; it is devoid of the intrinsic nature of existence and is like an illusion here.
A single drop of water fills a jar little by little, as it falls first and then gradually follows until the end;
even so, the mind that is first set upon the cause of supreme enlightenment gradually becomes a Buddha, perfected in pure qualities.
Practicing the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of phenomena, one does not touch nirvāṇa, nor does one course in signs;
just as a skilled boatman goes from this shore to the other shore, remaining neither on this side nor staying on that side in the midst of the ocean.
Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva does not conceive the thought: "I have been prophesied by the Ten-Powered Ones; I shall touch awakening.
Awakening does not become a source of fear, for there is nothing whatsoever here. Practicing in this way, one practices the wisdom of the Sugatas.
Seeing that the world is like a path through a wilderness, plagued by famine and disease, they put on their armor so as to have no further fear;
always mindful of the ultimate limit of existence, they do not allow even an atom of weariness to arise in their minds.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Sister Gaṅgadevā."
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the Victors, they know these aggregates to be unproduced and empty from the beginning;
though not in meditative equipoise, they look upon the realm of sentient beings with compassion, and in the meantime, they do not fall away from the qualities of a Buddha.

Just as a man who is skillful, endowed with all virtues, powerful, invincible, well-trained, and knowledgeable in the rules of the arts; who has reached the perfection of archery, possessed of manifold crafts, supreme in his knowledge of the methods of illusion, and desirous of the welfare of the world— Rgs_20.2.
Having taken his mother and father along with his wife and children, he sets out upon a wilderness path filled with many enemies;
having conjured many heroic and brave men, he returns home again in safety.
In the same way, at whatever time a wise Bodhisattva binds great loving-kindness to the entire realm of sentient beings,
having transcended the four Māras and the two levels, he remains established in this samādhi and yet does not touch awakening.
The wind rests upon space, and the mass of water rests upon that; upon this [water] rest the great earth and the world of beings.
It is solely due to the karma of sentient beings as the cause for their enjoyment; how could one conceive of this matter as being established in space?
In the very same way, this being established in emptiness displays various and manifold activities within the world;
yet it is solely through the empowerment of the beings' own wisdom and vows that [the Buddha] acts, and he does not touch upon extinction, for there is no place for emptiness to abide.
And at whatever time a wise and learned bodhisattva practices this supreme, peaceful samādhi of emptiness,
during that interval he should not manifest signs, nor should he abide in signlessness, practicing in peace and utter tranquility.
The bird has no footprint as it moves through the sky; it neither stands there nor does it fall to the ground.
In the same way, the bodhisattva practicing the gateway of liberation neither touches nirvāṇa nor dwells in the realm of signs.
Just as a man trained in archery, having shot one arrow, shoots another arrow after another in succession,
does not allow the first arrow to reach the ground, so that the arrow might fall only when the man desires it to fall— so it is with this.
In the very same way, while practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom and investigating wisdom, skillful means, power, and miraculous transformations,
one does not attain that ultimate emptiness so long as those roots of virtue are not yet fulfilled.
Just as a monk endowed with the power of supreme supernatural faculties, standing in the sky, performs twin miracles;
he displays walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting, yet he does not turn back nor does he grow weary as long as he remains there.
In the same way, the wise Bodhisattva, established in emptiness, having reached the perfection of knowledge and miraculous power, wanders without a fixed abode;
he displays infinite and diverse activities in the world, yet he is neither broken nor wearied for tens of millions of eons.
Just as some men, standing on the edge of a great precipice, might hold up two parasols with both hands and shield themselves;
even when a timely wind is released toward the great precipice, they do not fall into it until they have reached their destination there.

Abiding thus in compassion, the wise Bodhisattva, protected by the double umbrella of wisdom and skillful means, contemplates phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless; yet, practicing the Dharma, he does not touch nirvana.

Just as one who seeks jewels, having gone to the Isle of Jewels and obtained them, might return home again; although that caravan leader lives there in comfort, he is nonetheless distressed in mind for the sake of that multitude of people. (Rgs 20.15)
In the same way, having gone to the island of jewels that is emptiness and having obtained the powers, faculties, and meditations,
even if a bodhisattva touches nirvāṇa with joy, they still keep all suffering beings in mind.

Just as a merchant, knowing the way, travels through the interior of a city, a town, or a village for the sake of his desired goods, yet does not remain there, nor on the island of jewels, nor at home; so too the wise one becomes skilled in the path. Rgs 20.17.
In the same way, the wise Bodhisattva is skilled in all the knowledge of the Śrāvakas, their liberations, and their conditions;
yet he does not abide therein, nor in the Buddha-knowledge, nor in the conditioned—he is a knower of the path and one who understands its methods.

When one has bound compassion to the world and practices the meditative concentration of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—if such a person were to attain nirvāṇa, it would be impossible; or else, that conditioned state could indeed be designated.
Just as a magically created person has no visible body and cannot be designated by name,
so too a bodhisattva practicing the gateway of liberation cannot be designated by name.
If, when questioned, a bodhisattva does not practice the faculties nor provide an exposition of the profound Dharma—
the dharmas of irreversible awakening characterized by emptiness and signlessness— then one should know that he has not received the prophecy.
Even on the level of an Arhat or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, one does not touch the triple world even in a dream;
yet one sees Buddhas and speaks the Dharma to people—one should know that such a person is prophesied as irreversible.
Having perceived in a dream that beings have fallen into the three lower realms, they make a vow: "May I dry up those lower realms at that very moment.
By the empowerment of truth, they pacify that mass of fire; such a person should be known as one who has received the prophecy of non-retrogression.
Out of beneficial compassion, he pacifies various diseases caused by spirits and demons in the world of mortals through the power of his truth;
yet he does not give rise to conceit because of that, nor does he harbor pride, thinking "I am irreversible"—this one should be known as one who has received the prophecy.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twentieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Skill in Means."

Alternatively, if the conceit arises in him, "I have been prophesied," or "Various prosperities are accomplished through my empowerment of truth"—if another bodhisattva considers himself thus prophesied, one should know that this person of little intelligence stands in conceit. (Rgs 21.1)
Furthermore, Māra will approach and say: "This is your name;
it extends back through seven generations of your mother and father. When you become a Buddha, this shall be your name."
Whatever kind of ascetic conduct that practitioner of yoga will possess, these very qualities were already present in you previously.
Any bodhisattva who, having heard this, conceives pride, should be known as one of little intelligence, overcome by Māra.

When a Bodhisattva frequents remote villages and towns, mountain caves, wildernesses, and secluded forest retreats, yet draws himself down by disparaging others, one should know that a Mara of little intelligence has arisen within him. (Rgs 21.4)
They constantly dwell in villages, kingdoms, and towns, generating a longing for solitude;
yet, being intent on awakening and maturing sentient beings elsewhere, this is said to be the solitude of the Sugata’s sons.
If a bodhisattva dwells for many millions of years in mountain caves five hundred leagues wide, infested with wild beasts,
yet does not recognize this as solitude, he dwells in confusion, possessed by overweening pride.

He conceives pride toward those bodhisattvas who are devoted to the practice of walking meditation and have attained power, meditative concentrations, faculties, liberations, and absorptions, thinking:
"These are not those who dwell in the seclusion of the forest; this alone is the domain of seclusion spoken of by the Victor. Rgs 21.7.

Whether one dwells at the edge of a village or in the forest, free from the mind of the two vehicles and certain of supreme enlightenment—this is the solitude for those who have set out for the sake of the world; that bodhisattva would indeed measure himself against it. *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* 21.8.

In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra. Therefore, having destroyed pride, the wise person seeking supreme enlightenment with a resolute intention should, like a physician treating a patient's own disease, attend upon a spiritual friend without weariness. (Rgs 22.1)
The Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas who have set out for supreme enlightenment—these are the spiritual friends who have pointed out these perfections;
they are the instructors in this stage of practice, and by means of these two causes, one awakens to the enlightenment of a Buddha.
The Victors of the past and those yet to come, as well as all who dwell in every direction, have no other path than this perfection.
These perfections are taught as the illumination, the torch, the light, and the Teacher for those set out upon supreme enlightenment.
Just as the perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of emptiness, so too those who know all phenomena to have that same characteristic—
understanding phenomena through the characteristic of being empty of intrinsic nature— when they practice in this way, they practice the wisdom of the Sugatas.

Beings who desire food, conceptualizing it, wander in saṃsāra with minds attached; they always remember, "This is mine, this is my dharma. Both of these are unreal and empty; this knot of space is tied by the fool to himself.
Just as one who suspects poison comes to perceive it as such, yet that poison does not fall upon his stomach,
even so, this fool who has entered into my [teaching] is born and dies constantly, perceiving a self where none exists.
Just as grasping is, so has affliction and purification been explained by me; yet for me there is no apprehension of them.
For herein there is no one at all who is afflicted or purified; through wisdom, the Bodhisattva awakens to the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitā).

If all beings here in this entire Jambudvīpa were to generate the supreme mind of enlightenment, and for many billions of years give gifts and dedicate them all toward enlightenment for the sake of the world’s welfare; Rgs_22.8 //

But whoever here is devoted to the supreme perfection of wisdom and would practice it for even a single day, the mass of merit from that gift does not equal even a fraction of his; therefore, one should always apply oneself to wisdom with tireless diligence.
When the yogin practices the supreme perfection of wisdom, he generates great compassion yet remains free from the notion of a "sentient being.
Then that wise one becomes worthy of offerings for all the world, and he constantly partakes of the alms of the realm fruitfully.

The bodhisattva who desires here to liberate beings from the three miserable realms—beings who have long been Buddhas, gods, and humans—should show the broad path to the shore for the realm of beings, joined with the perfection of wisdom, day and night. Rgs 22.11.

Suppose a man who had never before obtained the foremost jewel were to find it again at a later time and be filled with joy; yet, having obtained it, he might lose it through negligence, and having lost it, he would remain in constant suffering, longing for that jewel. Rgs 22.12.

In the same way, one who has set out for the supreme enlightenment should not abandon the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, which is like a jewel; just as one who has found a jewel and holds it firmly, being undaunted, realizes its value and swiftly approaches safety. Rgs 22.13.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Spiritual Friend."
The sun rises, its garlands of rays dispelling all the darkness thick with gloom;
it outshines all the glow-worms and living beings, as well as the entire host of stars and the light of the moon.
In the same way, the wise Bodhisattva practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom dispels the thicket of views;
practicing emptiness and the signless, that vast Bodhisattva overcomes all the world and its secret conditions.

Just as a prince who bestows wealth and desires the welfare of others becomes the foremost among all those who approach him for aid—so too does he now liberate beings; how much more so when he has ascended the throne and wears the royal turban!
In the same way, the wise Bodhisattva who practices wisdom is a giver of the deathless nectar, beloved by gods and humans;
for he, devoted to the happiness of sentient beings, seeks it even before he has become established as the King of Dharma.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-third chapter, titled "Śakra."
At that time, Māra also becomes pierced by thorns, afflicted by grief, dejected in mind, and weakened in power;
he hurls meteors and sets the quarters ablaze to inspire fear, thinking, "How can this Bodhisattva become dejected in spirit? (Rgs 24.1)

When they become wise, endowed with pure intention, and day and night behold the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, then their body and mind will become like those of birds in flight; how then could that kinsman of Māra find an opportunity?

When Bodhisattvas fall into quarrels and disputes, their minds becoming hostile and mutually antagonistic, then Māra becomes exceedingly joyful and overjoyed, thinking: "They will both remain far removed from the wisdom of the Victors. (Rgs 24.3)
Both will become far removed from it, like *piśāca* demons; both will bring about the loss of their own vows.
For those who are wicked and devoid of patience, how can there be awakening? Then Māra, together with his faction, becomes joyful.
If a bodhisattva who has received this prediction should harbor malice toward one who has received the prediction and engage in a dispute,
for as many moments of thought as are associated with the fault of stubbornness, for that many eons must they once again don their armor.
Then the thought occurs to him: "The Buddhas touch enlightenment through the perfection of patience, which is not unwholesome.
He demonstrates the future restraints again, and whether he withdraws or departs, he trains here in the Buddha-dharma.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "On Overweening Pride."
The one who, as a trainee, does not approach anything at all as training, nor finds a teacher, nor even the dharmas of training;
who, without conceptualizing either training or non-training, practices—such a person trains here in the Buddha-dharma.
The bodhisattva who understands this training in this way is never deficient in training or immoral;
having mastered the Buddha-dharmas here, he trains in them, being skilled in the higher training and free from objective apprehension.
Let the wise indeed train in the teachings of those who radiate the light of wisdom; not even a single unwholesome thought arises in them.
Just as when the sun moves through the sky in the atmosphere, its rays do not remain, and the darkness before it vanishes.
When one is trained in the perfection of wisdom, all the perfections here become included within it;
just as the sixty-two views and the two [extreme] views are contained therein, so too do the perfections exist.
Just as when the life-faculty has ceased, all other various faculties that exist likewise cease;
even so, for the wise who practice the conduct of wisdom, it is said that all these perfections are included therein.
The wise Bodhisattvas train in all the qualities of the Śrāvakas as well as those of the Pratyekabuddhas;
yet, though they abide therein, they do not crave them. This is their training in the thought that must be cultivated—this is the meaning they train in.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Training."

If one rejoices with a sincere intention in the production of the thought of one who has set out for supreme enlightenment and is irreversible, that merit would be immeasurable even if compared to Mount Meru in the three-thousandfold world system; indeed, it cannot be measured against the merit of such rejoicing.
However many beings there may be who seek the wholesome and desire liberation, they all shall rejoice in this mass of merit.
Having attained the infinite qualities of a Victor for the sake of beings, they will bestow the Dharma upon the world for the exhaustion of suffering.

The bodhisattva who, being non-conceptual, thoroughly understands all phenomena as empty, signless, and beyond proliferation, and who does not seek awakening through a [grasping] intention—he is the yogi joined to the supreme perfection of wisdom. Rgs_26.3 //

There can be no contradiction between the element of space and the sky; for how could one ever encounter the other? In the same way, the wise Bodhisattva who practices wisdom is like the open sky, moving in tranquility.
Just as it does not occur to a man who is a magician that "these disciples perceive me," yet he performs his work;
they see him displaying various activities, yet he has no body, no mind, and no name.
In the same way, one who practices with wisdom never ceases; having awakened to enlightenment, they liberate the world.
They manifest various births and the application of diverse activities, appearing like an illusion, yet they do not wander in conceptual construction.
Just as a Buddha’s emanation performs the work of a Buddha yet feels no pride in doing anything at all,
even so the wise Bodhisattva who practices with wisdom displays all actions as being like a magical creation.
Just as a skilled carpenter has fashioned a wooden machine that performs every task like a man or a woman,
even so the wise Bodhisattva who conducts himself with wisdom performs all activities through knowledge, free from conceptual construction.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Simile of Illusion."
Thus do the wise ones, the vast assemblies of deities, bow with palms joined in reverence;
even all the Buddhas throughout the world-systems in the ten directions proclaim their praise of their excellent qualities.
Even if all the beings in as many fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were each to become Māras,
and if each single pore of the Bodhisattva were to manifest as many more, they would all be unable to create an obstacle for the wise one.
By four causes, the wise Bodhisattva becomes powerful, invincible, and unshakable by the four Māras;
he dwells in emptiness yet does not abandon sentient beings, remaining in a state that follows compassion for beings just as he has spoken.
The bodhisattva who has faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, the mother of the Tathāgatas as it is being taught,
and who applies himself to its practice with a resolute intention, should be known as one who has set out for omniscience.

He does not find a place within the suchness of the realm of phenomena; rather, he swiftly becomes non-abiding in the sky, like a vidyādhara suspended in the forest with his intent upon the woods—a tree in the air, untimely, empowered by the force of mantra. (Rgs 27.5)
Practicing in this way, the wise and learned bodhisattva perceives neither the one who awakens nor the qualities of a Buddha;
he perceives neither the teacher nor the seer within the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)—this is the dwelling of those seeking peace, who delight in its virtues.

Whatever dwellings there are of the Śrāvakas who possess confidence—those peaceful states associated with the bliss of tranquil meditative absorption—with the exception of the Arhat’s liberation, this dwelling of the Tathāgatas is supreme among them all and unsurpassed. (Rgs 27.7)
A bird dwells in the sky yet does not fall; a fish dwells in the midst of water yet does not die.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva who has reached the further shore of the power of meditation dwells in emptiness and yet does not attain final extinction.

Whoever wishes to go to the pinnacle of all the qualities of sentient beings and touch the supreme, most wonderful wisdom of a Buddha, should give the foremost, excellent, and sublime gift of Dharma; they should cultivate this foremost dwelling of those who bring benefit.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Essence."
Whatever trainings have been illuminated by the Guide, this training is the foremost and unsurpassed among them all.
Whoever wishes to reach the further shore of all trainings should train in this perfection of wisdom, the training of the Buddhas.
This is the supreme treasure, the treasury of the highest Dharma, the source of the lineage of the Buddhas, and a storehouse of bliss and happiness.
The Lords of the World in the ten directions—past and future alike—are born from this; yet the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is never exhausted.

As many trees, fruits, flowers, and forest plants as there are, all of which have arisen and appeared from the earth—the earth itself undergoes neither depletion nor increase; it does not weary, nor does it diminish, for it is free from conceptual construction.

As many Buddhas as there are, as well as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all the gods, and whatever qualities of happiness and bliss exist for all the world—all these are born from the supreme perfection of wisdom; yet this wisdom never diminishes, nor does it ever increase.
However many beings there are in the world—whether weak, middling, or superior—the Sugata has declared them all to arise from ignorance.
The machinery of suffering functions through the conjunction of conditions; yet that machinery is not exhausted, nor does ignorance increase.
As many gateways of the methods of knowledge as there are, all rooted in effort, are born from the supreme perfection of wisdom;
the mechanism of knowledge functions through the assembly of conditions, yet the perfection of wisdom neither increases nor decreases.

But the bodhisattva who understands this wisdom as inexhaustible for the sake of the non-arising of dependent origination—he, like the sun with its rays released from the mass of clouds, becomes a self-arisen one (svayaṃbhū) having dispelled the veil of ignorance. Rgs 28.7.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Scattering of Flowers."
Those of great power dwell in the four meditative concentrations, yet they form neither attachment nor reliance upon them;
nevertheless, these four concentrations with their constituent parts will serve as the support for attaining supreme, excellent enlightenment.
Abiding here in meditation, one becomes a possessor of excellent wisdom; the four formless and the four form meditative concentrations are supreme.
These meditations are beneficial for the most excellent enlightenment, yet a bodhisattva who trains in them does not undergo the destruction of the outflows.
This is a marvel, a wonder: amidst the accumulation of virtues, they dwell in meditative concentration where no signs exist.
Even if the physical body of those established therein should perish, they are reborn in the realm of desire according to their own intention.
Just as a person from Jambudvīpa, having never before obtained it, might reach the supreme city of the gods in heaven;
and having seen those realms there and taken possession of them, he would return again and not make his home there.
In the same way, those excellent bodhisattvas who possess virtuous qualities, having applied themselves to yoga and dwelling in meditative concentration and absorption,
again become established in the realm of desire, yet remain unstained— like a lotus in water— and are not dependent upon the ways of the foolish.

Except for the sake of maturing sentient beings, purifying the field, and fulfilling [the perfections], these great-souled ones do not pray for rebirth in the formless realm, where there would be no loss of the qualities of enlightenment and the perfections.
Just as if some man, having found a treasure of jewels, were not to conceive a mind of longing for it;
taking it alone at another time and entering his home, he would not be greedy.
In the very same way, having attained the four meditative concentrations and the peaceful samādhis that bestow joy and bliss, the wise Bodhisattvas relinquish the attainment of those meditative joys,
delights, and samādhis, and out of compassion for the world, they enter again into the realm of desire.

If a bodhisattva dwells in meditative concentration and dhyāna, yet does not give rise to a longing for the conditions of solitude, he becomes unconcentrated, with a mind that is agitated and scattered; his qualities of wisdom are lost, like a boatman whose ship has broken apart.

Furthermore, although he possesses the five strands of sensual pleasure—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—he is a bodhisattva free from the conditions for attachment; this infinite hero should always be known as one who is in a state of meditative concentration. (Rgs 29.10)
For the sake of other beings and persons, these pure beings wander about, devoted to the perfections of vigor and power;
just as a slave-girl has no autonomy over her own master, so do the steadfast ones come under the influence of all sentient beings.
And the female slave does not give a retort to her master, even when she is reviled or constantly beaten;
with a mind utterly terrified and overcome by fear, she thinks: "He will kill me for this reason."
In the same way, a bodhisattva who has set out for supreme enlightenment may remain throughout the entire world like a servant;
yet, upon the attainment of enlightenment and the fulfillment of all qualities, he consumes that very world just as fire born from grass and wood burns them up.
Having renounced their own well-being for the sake of the work of other beings, they apply themselves day and night with a mind free from expectation;
like a mother tending to an only son, they attend to them without weariness in their resolute intention.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Following."

The bodhisattva who intends to wander for a long time in saṃsāra for the sake of sentient beings, who is devoted to the yoga of purifying the buddha-fields, and who does not conceive even an atom of weariness—that one is endowed with the perfection of vigor and is untiring. Rgs 30.1.

Even if a wise bodhisattva were to count millions of eons, thinking that awakening has been attained after a long time through suffering—thinking that practicing the Dharma will entail long-lasting suffering—that person is deficient in the perfection of vigor and is of a lazy nature. Rgs 30.2.

From the very first moment of generating the mind set upon supreme enlightenment, until one attains unsurpassed peace, one should dwell upon that with a single-minded focus day and night; such a wise and learned person is to be known as one whose vigor has been initiated.

Even if someone were to say, "Only after splitting Mount Sumeru and going beyond it shall you attain supreme enlightenment," and if the Bodhisattva then conceives a sense of weariness or a sense of limitation, at that moment he has fallen into indolence.
Then this thought arises in him: "How much more so could even a tiny amount, for just a moment, reduce Sumeru to ashes?
With such initiating vigor, the wise Bodhisattva will before long attain the supreme enlightenment of the Leaders.
If one were to exert oneself through body, mind, and speech to bring the world to maturity and accomplish its welfare,
yet remains fallen into indolence due to the notion of a self— being far removed from the cultivation of selflessness like the sky is from the earth— [that effort is in vain].
In which there is neither body nor mind, nor the notion of a sentient being, but where one stands with the reversal of all notions, practicing the non-dual Dharma—
this is called the perfection of vigor by the Benefactor, for one who desires auspicious, unchanging, supreme enlightenment.

Having heard harsh words or ill-spoken speech from others, the wise Bodhisattva finds great joy; for what wise one would be attached to the supreme perfection of patience, considering who speaks, who hears, where, whose, or by what means? Rgs_30.8.

The Bodhisattva who is endowed with the qualities of virtue possesses such patience that even if one were to give away a triple-thousand world system filled with jewels to Buddhas—the World-Knowers, Arhats, and Pratyekabuddhas—the merit of that gift would not equal even a fraction of the merit in this [patience]. (Rgs 30.9)
For one who abides in patience, the physical body is completely purified, possessing the splendor of the thirty-two marks and being infinite and boundless.
By observing the empty and supreme Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, the wise one who practices patience becomes beloved throughout the entire world.
If some being, out of deep love and respect, were to take a casket of sandalwood and scatter it over a Bodhisattva,
and another were to throw a blazing fire upon his head, he should regard both acts as equal.

Having thus practiced patience, the wise and learned Bodhisattva dedicates that mental production toward supreme enlightenment; as many as are the instances of patience within the realm of sentient beings and their private conditions, the hero who practices patience surpasses them all throughout the entire world.

Even while practicing patience, one must again arouse the thought: "Having experienced many sufferings in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama—all caused by sensual pleasures and occurring against my will—why should I not today practice patience for the sake of enlightenment? Rgs 30.13.

Whether it be the lash of a whip, weapons, execution, imprisonment, or beating; whether it be the cutting off of the head, or the severing of the ears, feet, hands, or nose—I shall endure all the sufferings that exist in the world. Thus the Bodhisattva abides in the perfection of patience.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the thirtieth chapter, titled "Sadāprarudita."
Through ethical discipline they become exalted, desiring meditative concentration; established in the sphere of activity of those who possess the ten powers, their morality remains unimpaired.
To whatever extent they follow the practices of restraint, they dedicate all that for the benefit of all beings and for awakening.
If one who lacks faith in the conditions for enlightenment conceives a longing for it, yet remains immoral and acts with flaws before the wise,
but then dedicates that toward supreme, auspicious enlightenment while remaining possessed of the qualities of sensual desire, they abide in the perfection of ethical discipline.
That quality which is the attainment of the virtues of enlightenment for those who are gentle, and which consists of the dharmas of ethical discipline for those endowed with virtuous qualities—
yet that dharma which causes the loss of the virtues of enlightenment for those who act for the benefit of others, the Leader has declared to be immorality.
If a bodhisattva enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure, yet has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Saṅgha,
and keeps omniscience in mind, that wise one should be known as established in the perfection of ethical discipline.

If, while practicing for ten million eons through the ten paths of wholesome action, one generates a longing for the state of a Pratyekabuddha or an Arhat, then one becomes one of broken morality and flawed morality; this mental state is a more serious defeat than a *pārājika* offense.

Guarding their ethical discipline, they dedicate it toward supreme enlightenment; yet they do not conceive pride because of it, nor do they disparage themselves. Having abandoned the notion of a self and the notion of a sentient being, the bodhisattva who abides thus is said to be established in the perfection of ethical discipline.

If a bodhisattva, while practicing the path of the Victors, treats these virtuous beings as if they were unvirtuous, being ensnared by the perception of diversity, he is supremely unvirtuous; even if his conduct has flaws, he does not possess pure morality.

For one who has no perception of a self and no perception of a sentient being, how could there be non-restraint for one who is free from such perceptions? For one who has neither the conceit of restraint nor the conceit of non-restraint—this is the discipline of ethical conduct revealed by the Guide.
One who is thus endowed with ethical discipline, free from conceptual proliferation, and indifferent toward all things pleasant and unpleasant;
one who gives away head, hands, and feet with an undaunted mind, becomes a constant giver of all possessions, never shrinking back.
Having understood the nature of phenomena to be empty and selfless, one who possesses an undaunted mind does not cling even to their own flesh;
how much less would they fail to give away external objects? It is impossible that such a person would act out of stinginess.
But for those who perceive "mine," possessiveness and passion arise; how could they have the thought of renunciation?
Such people are fools. Through stinginess, they are reborn as pretas, or else they become poor among humans. (Rgs 31.11)
Then, having recognized these poor beings, the Bodhisattva becomes intent on giving and is always liberated in renunciation;
having given away the four continents adorned with all their splendors as if they were a mere lump of spittle, he does not become elated even upon obtaining those continents.

Having given a gift, the wise and learned Bodhisattva, having taken into account as many beings as there are in the three worlds, considers that this gift has been given to them all; and for the sake of the world, he dedicates that toward supreme enlightenment.
Having given a gift, the wise one does not rely on any object, nor does he ever expect a karmic result.
