By relinquishing in this way, the wise one becomes a renouncer of all; by giving a little, he obtains much that is immeasurable.
If all the beings who exist in their entirety throughout the three worlds were to give gifts for infinite eons;

and if the wise one, having gazed upon the Buddhas, were to calculate all the qualities of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas as well as the qualities of the Śrāvakas in their respective places— [the merit of the former would not equal even a fraction of the latter].

The wise Bodhisattva who is skilled in means, having rejoiced in those bases of meritorious action, should dedicate them for the sake of beings toward supreme, excellent enlightenment; thus engaged in dedication, he surpasses the entire world.
Just as a single great Vaiḍūrya gem outshines a vast heap of glass or ordinary jewels,
even so does a Bodhisattva who has perfected all dedications outshine the entire world’s vast heap of generosity.
If a bodhisattva, while giving a gift to the world, does not conceive a sense of "mine" therein nor any attachment to the object,
then his root of virtue increases in great majesty, like the orb of light of the moon during the bright fortnight.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dharmodgata."
By means of generosity, the bodhisattva cuts off rebirth as a hungry ghost; likewise, he cuts off poverty and all afflictions.
While practicing generosity, he obtains infinite and vast enjoyments, and brings to maturity those beings who have fallen into hardship.
Through ethical discipline, one avoids the various animal realms and the eight unfavorable conditions, and always attains the favorable conditions.
Through patience, one attains a supreme and magnificent form, with a golden complexion, beloved by the world and worthy of being gazed upon.
Through diligence, one does not undergo the loss of pure qualities; one attains infinite wisdom, the treasury of the Victor’s storehouse.
Through meditative concentration, one casts off the loathsome strands of sensual desire; through knowledge, one brings forth the superknowledges and samādhi.
Having fully understood the nature of phenomena through wisdom, one transcends the three realms and the lower states of existence.
Having turned the precious wheel of those who are bulls among men, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the exhaustion of suffering in the world.
Having fulfilled these qualities, that bodhisattva also embraces the purification of the field and the purification of sentient beings;
he embraces the lineage of the Buddhas, as well as the lineage of the Dharma and the lineage of the Saṅgha—indeed, all phenomena.
The supreme physician in the world who heals disease has proclaimed this path to awakening through the instruction of wisdom;
by name it is the "Accumulation of Precious Qualities," the path to awakening—may all sentient beings enter and attain this path.
In the *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, this is the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Entrustment."
[The Eulogy composed by Ācārya Haribhadra:
In order to lead the world easily to the path that carries the two kinds of excellence, the Blessed Buddha, whose mind was imbued with compassion, illuminated this [teaching].

Having heard this Sūtra, which is the abode of the reality of all phenomena, may those who have come here take it up and, having gone to their own place, burn away their impurities day and night. (Rgs_HPr_1)

In this present age of the Kali, crowded with many false views and when even the correct reading has long since departed, I have now—having observed the various discrepancies in the verses found in numerous manuscripts—properly restored this well-composed [text] for the benefit of the world by me, a "Bhadra," like Hari who cleared the well for the sake of the world; let it be accepted by the wise as the crushing of the frontal globes of the lordly elephants of disputants.
The *Bhagavatī Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, following the sequence of the chapters of the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, is completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

[The Colophon of the Scribe] O Buddhas who have gone to the sublime realms and O Bodhisattvas, please forgive me: if out of devotion I recite the Dharma spoken by the Sugata, yet somehow a word, a line of verse, or a single syllable is deficient in its prosodic measure; if through defects of the tongue, the movement of wind, or the influence of phlegmatic humors—O Buddhas, you who have reached the excellent abodes, may you grant forgiveness. (Rgs_LPr_1)
It is finished.
